executive_summary: World War II was the deadliest conflict in history: an estimated 60-75 million died, over half of them civilians, roughly 3% of the world's people in 1940. Two coalitions - the Allies and the Axis - fought across nearly every continent after a decade of appeasement and expansion. The war was won as much by industry and science as by battle: the US alone produced some 296,000 aircraft, while radar, penicillin, jet engines and the atomic bomb changed what war (and medicine and energy) could be. Its turning points clustered in 1942-43 - Midway, Stalingrad, El Alamein, Kursk - after which the Axis could only lose. The cost broke empires and built the modern order: the UN, the nuclear age, the Cold War, and the end of colonialism all descend from 1945. The deck argues this was the last world war not because there were no more wars, but because no conflict has since repeated its scale.
mode_note: No search MCP configured. Headline figures live-verified against Wikipedia REST API on 2026-09-12; secondary figures from internal encyclopedic knowledge, marked where estimates diverge. All contested numbers use conservative ranges with '~'.

verified_facts.claim: Total WWII deaths are estimated at 60-75 million, the deadliest conflict in history
Deaths represent about 3% of the estimated global population of 2.3 billion in 1940
Civilian deaths totaled 50-55 million; military deaths 21-25 million
The Holocaust murdered around 6 million Jews from 1941-1945, about two-thirds of Europe's Jews
The German 6th Army surrendered at Stalingrad, Feb 1943 - the largest and deadliest urban battle in history
At Midway 4-7 June 1942 the Japanese Combined Fleet lost four carriers - the decisive Pacific turning point
D-Day saw the largest seaborne invasion in history, 6 June 1944
Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, prompting the US declaration of war
Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, starting the war in Europe; Britain and France declared two days later
Germany invaded the USSR on 22 June 1941 (Operation Barbarossa)
The UN Charter was signed 26 June 1945; the United Nations had 51 founding members
'Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few.' - Churchill, House of Commons, 20 August 1940
The United States produced roughly 296,000 aircraft and 88,000+ tanks during the war
Soviet total war deaths ~27 million (military ~8.7M, civilian ~18M)
Over 100 million soldiers were mobilized in total across the war
The Iwo Jima flag-raising photograph was taken by Joe Rosenthal on 23 February 1945 (US Gov work, public domain)
sources: Wikipedia 'Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima' (Tier 2)

counter_evidence.claim: The 'Good War' framing is contested: Allied area-bombing of Dresden and Tokyo, the atomic bombs, and Soviet occupation brutality show the distinction between sides was not clean
counter_evidence.why_it_matters: Keeps the deck analytical rather than triumphal; supports the argument that the war's violence was total on every side

counter_evidence.claim: Casualty figures for China (15-25M range) and Germany (~7M disputed to ~13M) vary widely by source and counting method
counter_evidence.why_it_matters: The deck quotes ranges and uses '~', never a false precision

anecdotes.story: At Midway, US dive-bombers found the Japanese carriers refueling and rearming their fighters on deck; in a few minutes three carriers were burning, a fourth fell that evening.
anecdotes.why_it_works: Turns a strategic reversal into a single visual moment

anecdotes.story: Soviet factories rolled east by rail - 1,500 plants relocated beyond the Urals in 1941-42, many producing tanks and 100 days after arrival.
Britain's butter, sugar, meat and eggs were rationed from January 1940; the last ration (meat) ended only in July 1954.
anecdotes.why_it_works: A concrete, human measure of how long the war's shadow lasted
